                                                                                              Preface

    This databook defines the structure and usage of the Synopsys® Security IP MACsec Single Port
    Automotive Compliant (AC) Security Module (DWC_macsec) core.

Audience
    This guide is intended for users who are familiar with the following specification:
        n    FIPS Publication 197 - Advanced Encryption Standard
        n    NIST SP 800-38A - Block Cipher Modes of Operation
        n    NIST SP 800-38D - Galois/Counter Mode (GCM) and GMAC
        n    ARM IHI 0024C - AMBA APB Protocol
        n    IEEE 802.1AE-2018 Standard
        n    IEEE 802.3-2018 Standard
        n    IEEE 802.1Q-2018 Standard

Export Control
    Some Synopsys® Security IP may be restricted for export by government encryption regulations.
    Government export licenses and/or reporting may be required by law prior to transfer of the technology. A
    compliance check by authorized personnel is needed prior to transfer, as requirements vary depending on
    the product and the locations involved.

Databook Organization
    The chapters of this databook are organized as follows:
        n    Chapter 1, “Product Overview”, provides an introduction to the DWC_macsec.
        n    Chapter 2, “Architecture”, provides architecture details of the DWC_macsec.
        n    Chapter 3, “Performance”, provides details about the performance settings.
        n    Chapter 4, “Parameter Descriptions”, provides descriptions of the configuration parameters.
        n    Chapter 5, “Signal Descriptions”, provides descriptions of the DWC_macsec signals.
        n    Chapter 6, “Register Descriptions”, provides the memory map of the DWC_macsec and descriptions
             of the programmable software registers.
        n    Appendix A, “Acronyms”, provides the list of acronyms used in this document.

1.1          General Product Description
     The DWC_macsec module is used for inline encryption/decryption and authentication of ethernet packets
     as defined by the IEEE 802.1AE Standard. The DWC_macsec module handles full line rate single port
     support for the IEEE 802.1AE Standard up to 100 Gb/s. The DWC_macsec provides encryption and
     authentication based on the AES-GCM algorithm, as specified in the NIST Special Publication 800-38D
     Recommendation for Block Cipher Modes of Operation: Galois/Counter Mode (GCM) and GMAC of November 2007.
     The DWC_macsec is developed to be integrated between a MAC (Media Access Controller) and a Physical
     Coding Sublayer (PCS) or PHY, and it offers GMII, XGMII and XLGMII interfaces as defined in the IEEE
     802.3-2018 - IEEE Standard for Ethernet. Reduced interfaces such as RMII and RGMII are also supported
     and follow the RMII™ specification, RMII consortium, and Reduced Gigabit Media Independent Interface
     (RGMII) version 2.6 standards.
     The DWC_macsec is developed to minimize latency, by offering an optimized AES-GCM cryptographic
     core for TX/Egress and RX/Ingress paths. Several additional features are also present in the DWC_macsec,
     such as bypass mode, parametrizable amount of TX and RX secure channels and security associations,
     support for different VLAN TAG on the clear, separate APB interfaces for general configuration registers
     and AES critical registers.

1.2           Features
        n    Supports the following:
             q     IEEE 802.1AE-2018 Standard
             q     Frame Preemption (IEEE 802.1Qbu Standard) for lower performance data rates
             q     Up to 100 Gb/s for Egress path
             q     Up to 100 Gb/s for Ingress path
             q     Up to 32 secure channels for TX
             q     Up to 256 secure channels for RX
             q     Up to 64 secure associations for TX
             q     Up to 512 secure associations for RX
             q     Up to two VLAN TAGs on the clear (for Cisco Mode)
             q     VLAN TAG on the clear, copy and replace modes
             q     Jumbo frame
             q     Insertion and removal of SecTAG
             q     RGMII, RMII, SGMII, MII, GMII, XGMII and XLGMII interfaces
             q     APB for register access and key configuration
             q     Separate APB for AES-GCM register access and key configuration
             q     Asynchronous clock operation between TX and RX
             q     Asynchronous clock operation between APB and datapath clocks (TX, RX)
             q     Two rounds per clock for AES-GCM
             q     Area optimized Galois Field for AES-GCM
             q     Ternary Content Addressable Memory (TCAM) for security association search
             q     Direct or linear search modes for security association lookup
             q     FIPS 140-3 AES-GCM Test Mode
             q     Proprietary tagging for correctly received frames
             q     Configurable filtering rules for non-MACsec frames
             q     SRAM ECC
        n    Seamless integration with Synopsys Ethernet controllers and PCS modules

1.3           Roadmap Features Candidates Not Supported
    The following features are not supported for DWC_macsec in the current release:
        n    FIFO data streaming interfaces


                 Note     The not supported features could be part of a specific roadmap release. Reach out to Synopsys
                          for a complete roadmap description.

1.5           Reset Requirements
    The DWC_macsec has one reset signal, as shown in Figure 1-3.
        n     Power on Reset (pwr_on_rst): resets the complete IP
    Table 1-2 explains considerations for the reset connectivity.

                 clock domains


1.6           Memory Requirements
    The DWC_macsec has following memories:
        n     1x SRAM or TCAM for the Egress Channel/TX SAI (Secure Association Index) lookup
        n     1x SRAM for the Egress Channel/TX SAD (Secure Association) lookup
        n     1x SRAM for the Egress Channel/TX SA MIB data
        n     1x SRAM for the Egress Channel/TX SC (Secure Channel) MIB data
        n     1x SRAM or TCAM for the Ingress Channel/RX SAI lookup

        n    1x SRAM for the Ingress Channel/RX SAD lookup
        n    1x SRAM for the Ingress Channel/RX SA MIB data
        n    2x SRAM for the Ingress Channel/RX SC MIB data
        n    1x SRAM for the AES-GCM cipher key data
        n    1x SRAM for the AES-GCM hash key data
        n    1x SRAM for the AES-GCM hash context data
        n    1x SRAM for the AES-GCM cipher context data
     All external SRAM have a dedicated interface where the SoC integrator must connect their SRAM instances.
     All external SRAM interfaces operate in the tx_clk domain.

1.6.1         External SRAMs versus Internal Synthesizable Flip-Flops
     The memories can be external (SRAMs/TCAMs instantiated by the integrator and connected on the SoC) or
     internal (synthesizable Flip-Flops). The integrator decides if the memories are implemented in external
     SRAMs/TCAMs or internal synthesizable Flip-Flops (FFs).
     The internal/external implementation is configured by the parameters mentioned in the Table 1-3:

1.6.2             Memory Sizes
    The memory requirements are dependent by the following parameters:
         n       DWC_MACSEC_AES_MAX_KEY_SIZE: The maximum AES-GCM key size selection is 128 or 256
                 bits.
         n       DWC_MACSEC_TX_NUM_SC_SUPPORTED: The maximum amount of TX Secure Channels. This
                 influences the SRAMs depth associated with the Egress/TX.
         n       DWC_MACSEC_RX_NUM_SA_SUPPORTED: The maximum amount of RX secure associations.
                 This influences the SRAMs depth associated with the Ingress/RX.

    CoreConsultant to enable internal flip-flops. Table 1-4 also describes memory sizes calculation that can be
    used as Flip-Flop count estimate.

1.6.3         Memory Access Timings
    Figure 1-4 shows memory timings that must be adhered when instantiating technology-specific memory
    instances. Different memories can be configured depending on the selected configuration of the
    DWC_macsec.
        n    Single Port SRAM
             q     External SRAM containing just one single port, that is used for reading or writing.
        n    Two Port SRAM
             q     External SRAM containing one port for reading and one port for writing.
             q     Read and write ports use the tx_clk.
        n    Dual Port SRAM
             q     External SRAM containing two ports that can be used for Read+Read, Read+Write or
                   Write+Write parallel operations.
             q     Read and write ports use the tx_clk.
        n    Ternary Content Addressable Memory (TCAM)
             q     External SRAM that contains a Key input to be matched port, a Mask input port, a read/write
                   port and a Key search hit output port.
             q     Key search and read/write port use tx_clk.

1.8           Frame Preemption Usage Requirements
1.8.1         Initial setup
    When the PHY_MAP bit in the MIB_VALIDATE register is set, all non-MACsec frames are poisoned.
    Therefore, do not set this bit in the initial setup phase so that response frames can pass through MACsec,
    which enables frame preemption.

1.8.2         Data Modes
    Frame Preemption is supported for all performance modes.



Version 6585-001                                               Synopsys, Inc.                                    SolvNetPlus    27
March 2025                                                                                                       Synopsys IP
Product Overview                                              MACsec Single Port Automotive Compliant (AC) Security Module Databook



1.8.3         Fragment Sizes
     Frame Preemption is only supported for ingress Tx fragments size equal to or higher than 70 bytes
     (including CRC).
     Rx MAC controller must accept fragment sizes equal to or higher than 48 bytes (including CRC). For more
     information on configuring fragment sizes, see Ethernet MAC controller Databook.

1.9           System Integration
     This section describes the integration of the DWC_macsec within a SoC.

1.9.1         Parameter Dependency versus the Ethernet Controller
     Table 1-6 describes the DWC_macsec parameter dependencies towards the Ethernet Controller.
Table 1-6       Parameter with Ethernet Controller Dependencies

      Parameter                  Description

      DWC_MACSEC_PERF_RATE This parameter selects the maximum throughput supported by the DWC_macsec and
                           the associated data interface. The interface needs to match the one interface used in
                           the Ethernet Controller.

      DWC_MACSEC_DUAL_IF         This parameter when enabled, generates a DWC_macsec IP that contains two
                                 interfaces: GMII and XGMII. This allows the integrator to connect both to the MAC and
                                 PCS, and then at boot time select which interface (and associated throughput) is to be
                                 used.


1.9.2         Interfaces Integration Overview
     The signal list described in Chapter 5, “Signal Descriptions” is grouped into functional interfaces, so it is
     easier to depict the complete module integration. The interface grouping shown in Figure 1-9 follows the
     same interface/signal grouping described in Chapter 5, “Signal Descriptions”.
     This integration example describes an inline MACsec AC operation solution between the Ethernet
     Controller (MAC) and an Ethernet PHY or PCS.
     Figure 1-9 shows the types of interfaces avaliable for the DWC_macsec integration.
        n    A - Interfaces for the Ethernet Controller and PHY (or PCS): It is shown in Figure 1-9 as the direct
             connections to the MAC and PCS.
        n    B - Functional Interfaces to the System: All the interfaces that are connected to the SoC
             infrastructure, containing APB interfaces and interrupts and register access lock signals. The
             integrator finds the most suitable connection scheme for these interfaces for the targeted SoC.
        n    C- Clocks and Resets: It is shown in Figure 1-9 as the Clock and Reset Signals group containing all
             clocks and reset signals. The integrator follows the considerations described in “Clock Requirements”
             on page 14 and “Reset Requirements” on page 15.

        Synopsys IP                                                                                                     March 2025
MACsec Single Port Automotive Compliant (AC) Security Module Databook                                                                          Product Overview



        n      D - Interfaces for the External Memories: It is shown in Figure 1-9 as AES-GCM SRAM Interfaces,
               TX/Egress SRAM Interfaces and RX/Ingress SRAM Interfaces (available when memories are
               selected as not synthesizable logic). The integrator must connect these specific interfaces to their
               specific memory/SRAM components, if internal synthesizable flip-flops are not selected by
               configuration options.

1.9.3            System Integration Overview
    Figure 1-10 shows the complete integration of the DWC_macsec with a Synopsys Ethernet MAC and
    Synopsys PCS.

1.9.3.1             Data Interfaces
    The Ethernet data interfaces are connected directly to the Ethernet MAC and Ethernet PCS/PHY. The
    interfaces used are standard IEEE type of interfaces. The clock used for the rx_clk is the one provided by
    the PHY while the clock used for the tx_clk is under control by the DWC_macsec (but must be the same
    clock used by the Ethernet MAC TX).




Version 6585-001                                                       Synopsys, Inc.                                                      SolvNetPlus       29
March 2025                                                                                                                                 Synopsys IP
Product Overview                                            MACsec Single Port Automotive Compliant (AC) Security Module Databook



1.9.3.2         Clock and Reset
     The DWC_macsec operates most of the logic with the tx_clk. The tx_clk is used for the Egress GMII
     interface. Therefore, it must be the same source as the one used to generate the GMII, XGMII, XLGMII data
     for the Ethernet MAC Egress path.
     The rx_clk is provided by the PHY and with this clock the Ingress GMII, XGMII, XLGMII interface is
     processed and passed to the Ethernet MAC. Therefore, the same clock source must be used for the Ingress
     path of the Ethernet MAC.
     The DWC_macsec has one reset source that resets the complete IP.
     The reset source should not be connected to any bypass selector, to avoid any security pitfalls. For example,
     it is not possible to reset the IP and at the same time select a bypass path that allows the data to be
     propagated on-the-clear/without encryption/authentication.

1.9.3.3         System Interfaces
     The APB interfaces can be directly connected to the system. These are used to configure the DWC_macsec
     control registers and program the keys used with the AES-GCM. It is suggested that the AES-GCM APB is
     connected directly to a trusted module such as embedded HSM/SE to mitigate security issues.
     The associated PPROT signals of the APB must be used to control the access to the DWC_macsec registers,
     and all accesses must be secure (meaning PPROT signals driven with 0).

1.9.3.4         SRAM Interfaces
     The DWC_macsec products needs several SRAMs to store AES-GCM specific hash and cipher intermediate
     data, as well SRAMs to store Egress/Ingress lookup databases and MIB data. The DWC_masec provides the
     SRAM interfaces, but the SRAMs must be instantiated by the integrator.

1.9.4         Automotive Support Overview
     The DWC_macsec AC is an ASIL-B for random hardware faults product. It implements the following safety
     packages:
        n    Internal Safety Mechanisms (SMs)
        n    Failure Modes, Effects, and Diagnostic Analysis (FMEDA)
        n    Design Failure Mode and Effect Analysis (DFMEA)
     The MACsec automotive-compliant security module safety documentation includes the following (but is
     not limited to):
        n    FMEDA report
        n    DFMEA report
        n    Safety manual

1.9.4.1         DWC_macsec Automotive Safety Mechanisms
     The following section describes the external and internal safety mechanisms.




30      SolvNetPlus                                 Synopsys, Inc.                                              Version 6585-001
        Synopsys IP                                                                                                   March 2025
MACsec Single Port Automotive Compliant (AC) Security Module Databook                                Product Overview



1.9.4.1.1          Internal Safety Mechanism
    The DWC_macsec ASIL-B has several internal safety mechanisms that monitor transient and permanent
    faults. The following list provides a summary of the safety mechanisms:
        n    Parity protection for the main data and control signals.
        n    Parity protection for the APB transactions
        n    Configuration register duplications for all available registers.
        n    SRAM ECC for writing and reading SRAM data and addresses.
        n    Latency managers monitor datapath stalling errors.
        n    CRC imposes a standard feature that is used for ingress or egress ethernet frame validation.
        n    RX Message Authentication Code (MAC) imposes a standard feature that is used as end-to-end
             protection for AES-GCM.
        n    AES-GCM Built-in Self-Test (BIST) for detecting latent permanent faults.
        n    Lock step for detecting single permanent faults in AES-GCM.
        n    Timing redundancy (TR) for detecting single permanent faults in AES-GCM.
        n    AES-GCM FIPS firmware-driven test for detecting latent permanent faults.
        n    Dual modular redundancy for critical blocks.
        n    Triple modular redundancy for certain features or blocks.
        n    Dual rail protection for detecting faults in critical input signals.
        n    Alarms dual rail for detecting faults in critical output signals.
        n    Several error injection mechanisms for parity, ECC, duplication, and so on.

1.9.4.1.2          External Safety Mechanism
    The DWC_macsec ASIL-B depends on several external safety mechanisms to obtain the ASIL-B random
    fault metrics. The following list provides a summary of the safety mechanisms:
        n    SRAM ECC check to detect any ECC errors when DWC_macsec is accessing the external SRAMs.
        n    Parity protection for the APB transactions.
        n    Logical BIST detects permanent faults through logical testing at startup.
        n    APB register read back to detect faults in configuration registers.
        n    APB watchdog timer detects faults in configuration registers.
        n    Key monitors (TX or RX external key monitors).
        n    Error injection mechanisms for all safety mechanisms.

2.1            Architecture Overview
2.1.1          General Description
     The DWC_macsec module contain the following main sub-parts: TX/Egress channel, RX/Ingress channel,
     and the AES-GCM cryptographic core, as shown in Figure 2-1. The AES-GCM cryptographic core
     throughput is dimensioned to serve both TX/Egress and RX/Ingress channels without any performance
     drop or stalling.
     The DWC_macsec data interfaces are GMII, XGMII or XLGMII. These interfaces can be plug-and-play in a
     seamless way into a system with an Ethernet MAC and Ethernet PHY/PCS. The configuration of the
     DWC_macsec is done by two APB interfaces: one for the general purpose MACsec AC registers and one for
     the specific AES-GCM registers and keys.
     The system features two independent interrupt lines that can be connected to an interrupt system, which
     can be used to monitor several error conditions.
     All the SRAM components need to be integrated at SoC level as the DWC_macsec does not provide built-in
     SRAM wrappers or SRAM components. There is nonetheless the possibility of replacing, by configuration
     options, some SRAMs by DWC_macsec internal Flip-Flop banks.

2.1.2           AES-GCM Cryptographic Core
    The DWC_macsec contains one 128-bit or 256-bit key size AES-GCM cryptographic engine. The datapath
    width for the AES-GCM core is linked to the overall throughput required for the selected MACsec AC
    performance. The integrator selects the wanted MACsec AC throughput, and the AES-GCM is dimensioned
    accordingly.
    The value set for the DWC_MACSEC_PERF_RATE automatically configures the datapath width of the AES-
    GCM engine, so it can encrypt/decrypt and authenticate the wanted line rate without performance drop or
    stalling.
    The AES-GCM can be configured to support 128-bit key size or 256-bit key size by the
    DWC_MACSEC_MAX_KEY_SIZE parameter.




Version 6585-001                                                   Synopsys, Inc.                                                       SolvNetPlus         49
March 2025                                                                                                                              Synopsys IP
Architecture                                                   MACsec Single Port Automotive Compliant (AC) Security Module Databook



2.1.3          TX/Egress Channel
     The TX/Egress channel receives the GMII, XGMII or XLGMII interface data from the Ethernet MAC.
     The data CRC is checked against any errors; errors are removed before data is fed to the AES-GCM. After
     the data is encrypted and the authentication Tag is generated by the AES-GCM, the packet CRC is again
     generated and appended to the data.
     The TX/Egress channel output GMII, XGMII or XLGMII interface should be connected to an Ethernet PCS
     or PHY. The TX/Egress channel performs the packet parsing rules as described in the IEEE 802.1AE
     Standard.

2.1.4          RX/Ingress Channel
     The RX/Ingress channel receives the GMII, XGMII or XLGMII interface data from the Ethernet PCS or PHY.
     The data CRC is checked against any errors; errors are removed before data is fed to the AES-GCM. After
     the data is decrypted and authenticated by the AES-GCM, the packet CRC is again generated and appended
     to the data.
     The RX/Ingress channel output GMII, XGMII or XLGMII interface should be connected to an Ethernet
     MAC. The RX/Ingress channel performs the packet parsing rules as described in the IEEE 802.1AE Standard.

2.1.5          Key Handling and Swapping
     The security association keys are installed into the AES-GCM core by the specific AES-GCM APB interface.
     The key installation bit and the integrator enable a key installation interrupt that is triggered when the AES-
     GCM finishes installing a key. Typically, a key installation on the AES-GCM is fast and is done under 30 TX
     clock cycles.
     Swapping keys for the AES-GCM is based on the principles of security association keys defined in the IEEE
     802.1AE Standard. The system is responsible for handling the active/inactive values for each security
     association. Programming a new key into an active security association of a specific security channel leads
     to unexpected behavior.

2.1.6          Bypass Encryption/Decryption
     The DWC_macsec bypass function allows unencrypted data to pass through the core. The DWC_macsec
     supports following types of bypass:
         n     Frame bypass when it does not match any Security Association on TX/RX.
               q   For example, if the packet does not have a match against the security association lookups, then
                   the packet is not encrypted/decrypted and/or authenticated.
         n     Static bypass of all frames when the specific bypass registers are set on TX/RX.
               q   This mode is used to perform system integration debugging; you can leave the SA databases
                   empty and pass traffic between the MAC and PCS.

2.1.7          Programming Interfaces
     The programming of DWC_macsec, including the AES keys, is done by two APB interfaces.




50      SolvNetPlus                                    Synopsys, Inc.                                              Version 6585-001
        Synopsys IP                                                                                                      March 2025
MACsec Single Port Automotive Compliant (AC) Security Module Databook                                     Architecture



2.1.8         Register Access
    The registers are accessed by a host APB interface, and an additional protection control exists to prevent non-
    secure accesses:
        n    The APB pprot[0] signals must be driven low so the APB interface can access any DWC_macsec
             registers.

2.2           Data Interfaces
    The DWC_macsec is connected to the Ethernet MAC and Ethernet PCS/PHY as shown in Figure 2-10. The
    data interfaces are divided in:
        n    xGMII Interfaces from Ethernet MAC: These contain the RMII, RGMII, MII, GMII, XGMII or
             XLGMII plain data interface for the Egress data and the RMII, RGMII, MII, GMII, XGMII or XLGMII
             plain data interface for the ingress data, that needs to be connected to the MAC.
        n    xGMII Interfaces to Ethernet PCS/PHY: These contain the RMII, RGMII, MII, GMII, XGMII or
             XLGMII secure data interface for the Egress data and the RMII, RGMII, MII, GMII, XGMII or XLGMII
             secure data interface for the ingress data, that need to be connected to the PCS/PHY.

2.2.1         Data Interfaces Signaling
    All the data interfaces are based on the xMII interface definition of the IEEE 802.3 Standard. Figure 2-10
    shows the DWC_macsec xGMII interface signals. The COL and CRS signals are not used, as the
    DWC_macsec always operates in full duplex mode.

2.2.2         Data Interfaces and CRC
    The DWC_macsec is integrated between an Ethernet MAC and an Ethernet PCS/PHY. The CRC calculated
    by the MAC needs to be re-calculated in the Egress and Ingress paths after encryption and/or
    authentication takes place.
    The DWC_macsec recalculates the CRC as defined in the IEEE 802.3 Standard, and if a CRC error is
    identified, the packet is poised with a CRC error towards the Ethernet MAC. An interrupt can be triggered
    by the global interrupt line to the system (if enabled).


              Note        The DWC_macsec does not drop frames when a CRC error is detected.



    There are several variants included in the xGMII spectrum. The 802.3 standard defines the following:
        n    MII using a nominal 4-bit interface
        n    GMII using a nominal 8-bit interface
        n    XGMII using a nominal 32-bit interface
        n    XLGMII/CGMII using a nominal 64-bit interface
    But as these interfaces follow the same protocol, implementations of 128-bit XLGMII are also available to
    reduce clock frequencies.




Version 6585-001                                               Synopsys, Inc.                      SolvNetPlus     51
March 2025                                                                                         Synopsys IP
Architecture                                                     MACsec Single Port Automotive Compliant (AC) Security Module Databook




                        n   RGMII and RMII interfaces are widely used, but they are not covered by the IEEE 802.3
               Note         standard.
                        n   CGMII is another notation for 100 Gb/s XLGMII, which implies the use of a 128-bit
                            interface.


     As mentioned in the “General Product Description” section, the DWC_MACsec module is integrated
     between the MAC and PHY/PCS blocks, and communication is made through the xGMII data interfaces.
     The interfaces are split between the TX and RX paths, each having its associated control signals.
     In Figure 2-3, Figure 2-3, Figure 2-4, Figure 2-5, Figure 2-6, Figure 2-7, and Figure 2-8, the signal interface
     section details all the individual signals and buses that make up these interfaces.

2.3            Dual Interface configuration
     DWC_MACsec supports dual interface mode. When set at boot time, it enables the use of either an 8-bit
     GMII or a 128-bit XLGMII interface through the MACsec_IP_Control.data_mode configuration register.
     Depending on the selected performance rate (DWC_MACSEC_PERF_RATE), this allows for the support of
     different speed modes and, consequently, sub-interfaces of GMII (MII, RMII, RGMII) or XLGMII (32-bit
     XGMII, 64-bit XLGMII) respectively.

2.4           Security Associations Mode of Work
    This section describes how the security associations and security channels are parsed and evaluated, as per
    the values programmed into the SAI and SAD databases.

2.4.1         TX/Egress Security Associations Mode of Work
    The DWC_macsec TX/Egress SAI and SAD lookup behavior is shown in Figure 2-10. The packet received
    from the MAC is initially parsed against the SAI lookup table, and an associated TX SC index is extracted.
    This TX SC index is concatenated with the ACT_SA[x], and the final pointer to the TX SAD is created. The
    packet is then parsed against the configuration set on the TX SAD, that is pointed by the concatenated index.


              Note        The concatenation of the TX SC Index and ACT_SA[x] is nothing else than creating selecting
                          which SA is active for a given Security Channel.


    The AES-GCM key pointer is also extracted from the TX SC Index with the ACT_SA[x] concatenation. For
    more information on AES-GCM key programming and mapping, see “Programming a Key Context” on
    page 77.

2.4.1.1                          Programming the TX SAI, SAD and SALT Tables
      This section describes how to program the TX SAD, SAI, and SALT tables.

To program the TX SAD, the following steps must be performed:
            1.            Program the TX_SAD_0_LOW.
            2.            Program the TX_SAD_0_HIGH.
            3.            Program the TX_SAD_1_LOW.



      58                  SolvNetPlus                                                                                                                                                                                  Synopsys, Inc.                                                                                                                                                                    Version 6585-001
                          Synopsys IP                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          March 2025
MACsec Single Port Automotive Compliant (AC) Security Module Databook                                   Architecture



       4.    Program the TX_SAD_1_HIGH.


                 Note     The SAD register allocation versus bit-fields is described in
                          Figure 2-10.


       5.    Program the TX_SAD_2_LOW.
       6.    Program the TX_SAD_2_HIGH.
       7.    Program the TX_SAD_3_LOW.
       8.    Program the TX_SAD_3_HIGH.
       9.    Program the TX_PRG_SAD:
            a.     Set the SRAM entry number that must be loaded with the above values, by the
                   TX_PRG_SAD.ENTRY.
            b.     Set the indication in the TX_PRG_SAD.TYPE to indicate a write operation.


                 Note     The TX_ SAD_PRG needs to be programmed in a single APB write.



     10.     If a new entry needs to be programmed.
            a.     Poll the TX_SAD_PG.WR_BUSY and if 0, then go to step 1.

To program the TX SALT, the following steps must be performed:
       1.    Program the TX_SALT_TABLE_0.
       2.    Program the TX_SALT_TABLE_1.
       3.    Program the TX_SALT_TABLE_2.
       4.    Program the TX_SALT_PRG:
            a.     Set the SRAM entry number that must be loaded with the above values, by the
                   TX_SALT_PRG.ENTRY.
            b.     Set the indication in the TX_SALT_PRG.TYPE to indicate a write operation.
       5.    If a new entry needs to be programmed
            a.     Poll the TX_SALT_PG.WR_BUSY and if 0, then go to step 1.

To program the TX SAI, the following steps must be performed:
       1.    Program the TX_SRC_FILT_0.
       2.    Program the TX_SRC_FILT_1.
       3.    Program the TX_DST_FILT_0.
       4.    Program the TX_DST_FILT_1.



Version 6585-001                                               Synopsys, Inc.                    SolvNetPlus     59
March 2025                                                                                       Synopsys IP
Architecture                                                      MACsec Single Port Automotive Compliant (AC) Security Module Databook



        5.      Program the TX_LOOKUP_TABLE_VLAN_INFO.
        6.      Program the TX_SAI_OTHER_FIELDS register.
        7.      Program the TX_SAI_PRG:
               a.     Set the SRAM entry number that must be loaded with the above values, by the
                      TX_SAI_PRG.ENTRY.
               b.     Set the indication in the TX_SAI_PRG.TYPE to indicate a write operation.
        8.      If a new entry needs to be programmed.
               a.     Poll the TX_SAD_PG.WR_BUSY and if 0, then go to step #1.
        9.      Program the TX_ACTIVE_AN register.
               a.     This sets which TX ANs are active for the session, as shown in Figure 2-10.
               b.     This can be modified during mission mode with the objective of changing keys or to bring an
                      AN/SA down.


                    Note     Confidentiality offset is not supported in AES-GCM-XPN mode as per definition of the IEEE
                             802.1AE Standards. Therefore, the OFFSET field is not used when AES-GCM-XPN is enabled.



2.4.2               RX/Ingress Security Associations Mode of Work
     The DWC_macsec RX/Ingress SAI and SAD lookup behavior is shown in Figure 2-11. The packet received
     from the PCS/PHY is initially parsed against the SAI lookup table. If a match exists for a specific entry, then
     same entry number is taken for the SAD, SALT and Anti-Replay Window for further packet inspection.
     The AES-GCM key pointer is constructed taking into consideration the SAI SRAM entry hit plus a fixed
     offset (that is imposed by the amount of TX Security Associations). For more information on AES-GCM key
     programming and mapping, see “Programming a Key Context” on page 77.

                    Note   The RX_SAD_PRG needs to be programmed in a single APB write.



       8.       If a new entry needs to be programmed:
               a.    Poll the RX_SAD_PG.WR_BUSY and if 0, then go to step 1.

                     RX_SALT_PRG.ENTRY.
               b.    Set the indication in the RX_SALT_PRG.TYPE to indicate a write operation.

               a.    Poll the RX_SALT_PG.WR_BUSY and if 0, then go to step 1.

2.5              VLAN on the Clear Mode Support

    This section describes the supported modes by the DWC_macsec.

2.6            Inter Packet Gap (IPG) Considerations and MAC Programming
    The DWC_macsec is placed between an Ethernet MAC and an Ethernet PCS/PHY, the Inter Packet Gap at the output of the Ethernet MAC, is large
    enough for the DWC_macsec to add the SecTAG and ICV. Additionally, if the DWC_macsec is configured to operate with a VLAN on the clear
    mode, it may be necessary (depending on the mode) to increase even further the minimum TX IPG at the inputs of the DWC_macsec.
    Table 2-2 shows the input values of the DWC_macsec (column 6 and column 7), depending on the configured operation mode. The column of the
    VLAN Copy Mode indicates the following:
        n      None: no VLAN TAG is added by the DWC_macsec IP (represents the configuration space of the register MACsec_IP_Control.vlanmode =
               3'b000, 3'b001, 3'b101)
        n      Single: one additional VLAN TAG is inserted by the DWC_macsec IP (represents the configuration space of the register
               MACsec_IP_Control.vlanmode = 3'b011, 3'b100, 3'b110)
        n      Dual: two additional VLAN TAG are inserted by the DWC_macsec IP (represents the configuration space of the register
               MACsec_IP_Control.vlanmode = 3'b010)

2.7           KaY and Unknown Cipher Packet Handling
    The DWC MACsec standard defines the following modes of handling packets by a controlled port, imposed
    by TCI (Tag Control Information) field:
        n    Case 1: E = 0, C = 0 - packet to be authenticated with standard defined AES-GCM algorithm
        n    Case 2: E = 0, C = 1 - packet using other cipher suite
        n    Case 3: E = 1, C = 0 - KaY frames




Version 6585-001                                               Synopsys, Inc.                                 SolvNetPlus      71
March 2025                                                                                                    Synopsys IP
Architecture                                                   MACsec Single Port Automotive Compliant (AC) Security Module Databook



         n     Case 4: E = 1, C = 1 - packet to be authenticated and encrypted with standard defined AES-GCM
               algorithm
     Case 1 and Case 4 are handled by the DWC_macsec as defined by the standard:
         n     On the TX an association with an SA is complete, a SecTAG is created, ICV is calculated and if E = 1,
               the data payload is encrypted
         n     On the RX the packet is matched against an SA, the SecTAG is removed, ICV is checked and if E = 1,
               the data payload is decrypted
     Case 2 and Case 4 are handled as following:
         n     KaY frames are handled as per defined in the standard and the frames are not processed on the TX or
               RX. This allows the application to create KaY frames and transmit them unencrypted (with
               perspective of MACsec AC). When a frame is marked as KaY frame (E= 1, C = 0) on the TX or RX
               SAD, it is simply bypassed and sent to the PCS or MAC, respectively.
         n     Unknown Cipher frames are also handled as bypass frames. While there is not a direct applicability
               currently at the 802.1AE standard for an unknown cipher frame, it could be used to pass data
               between Uncontrolled Ports. For this, it is the responsibility of the application to create and parse
               these type of frames.

2.8            MIB Counters Usage
     The DWC_macsec contains several MIB (Management Information Base) counters. The following are the
     main types of MIB Counters:
         n     Security Association (SA) Monitoring Counters
         n     Security Channel (SA) Monitoring Counters
         n     Global Monitoring Counters
     All the counters need to be addressed indirectly by a command interface. This command interface is
     controlled by the following APB addressable registers:
         n     MIB_CMD
               q   This is the main command register, where you should configure the required action (for example,
                   read back TxUntaggedPkts_GBL).

         n     MIB_CMD_STAT
               q   This register indicates an ongoing operation.
         n     MIB_WR_DATA_HIGH
               q   This includes the MSB data registers where you can set a value that is written to the selected
                   counter. You can not only read but also set a counter value.
               q   Counter selection is done by the MIB_CMD register.
         n     MIB_WR_DATA_LOW
               q   This includes the MSB data registers where you can set a value that is written into the selected
                   counter. You can not only read but also set a counter value.




72      SolvNetPlus                                    Synopsys, Inc.                                              Version 6585-001
        Synopsys IP                                                                                                      March 2025
MACsec Single Port Automotive Compliant (AC) Security Module Databook                                                 Architecture



             q      Counter selection is done by the MIB_CMD register.
        n    MIB_CMD_D_BUF_HIGH/LOW_x (with x from 0 to 11)
             q      These registers read back data from the selected counter
                    n   Counter selection is done by the MIB_CMD register.
             q      Most of the counters are 64-bit wide. The data is divided into *_LOW and *_HIGH registers (if a
                    counter is only 32 bit, then only the *_LOW has valid data).
             q      In case of a counter read back: For a 64 bit counter, both _HIGH_ and _LOW_ have valid data,
                    and for a 32 bit counter only the _LOW_ has valid data.

                                The MIB counters should be all cleared after reset, by issuing an INIT command (see the
            Attention
                                sections below about the commands). This will set all the MIB stored in SRAMs to 0x0.

2.8.2         Accessing the MIB Counters
    The MIB Counters are addressed by a command interface, which is accessible by the Host ABP interface.
    To execute a read command, the firmware must:
        1.   Write to the MIB_CMD register with the command details.
        2.   Poll the BUSY field of MIB_CMD_STAT register. When the register field is low, the operation is
             finished.
        3.   Read back the results from the MIB_CMD_D_BUF_LOW/HIGH_x registers. Not all
             *_LOW/HIGH_x register indexes may contain valid data (depending on the executed command).
    To execute a write command, the firmware must:
        1.   Write the MIB_WR_DATA_LOW/HIGH with the wanted data.
        2.   Write to the MIB_CMD register with the command details.
        3.   Poll the BUSY field of MIB_CMD_STAT register. When the register field is low, the operation is
             finished.
    Table 2-6 describes the possible commands that can be requested by the MIB_CMD register.

2.8.3          MIB Counters Linking to Security Associations (SA) and Security Channels
     The MIB SA counters associated with TX and/or RX SAs, follow a direct mapping. The SAs programmed in
     the TX SAI in the Lookup entry 0, corresponds to the MIB Counters for Security Association 0. The same
     mapping method is applicable for RX SAI Lookup. Nonetheless, the RX Security Associations need to be
     mapped into specific MIB SC Counters, as for RX there isn´t any notion of which Security Association
     belongs to which security channel.
     The DWC_macsec allows you to select which RX Security Association maps to which security channel.



76      SolvNetPlus                                        Synopsys, Inc.                                              Version 6585-001
        Synopsys IP                                                                                                          March 2025
MACsec Single Port Automotive Compliant (AC) Security Module Databook                                         Architecture



    To perform the MIB Counter security channel linking with the respective Security Association, you must
    configure the association table:
        1.    Program the RX_SAI_SC_CORR_TABLE_SC_VALUE: with a value of a Security Channel.
        2.    Program the RX_SAI_SC_CORR_TABLE_PRG.
             a.    TYPE: set this field to 1'b1 to indicate a write access.
             b.    ENTRY: in this field one must write the Security Association number, that should be associated
                   with the Security Channel set on the _VALUE register above. As an example:
                   n     RX_SAI_SC_CORR_TABLE_SC_VALUE = 5 and ENTRY = 3.
                   n     This means that RX Security Association #3 belongs to the RX Security Channel #5. Thus,
                         when an event occurs on Security Association #3, the MIB counter(s) of Security Channel #5
                         are going to be incremented.
        3.    If another entry needs to be programmed:
             a.    Poll RX_SAI_SC_CORR_TABLE_PR.BUSY.
             b.    If 1'b0, then jump to Step 1.

2.9               Key Configuration and Key Swap
    This section describes how to program the keys into the AES cores and how to perform a key swap. Each
    key is considered as a context (also known as key context).

2.9.1         Programming a Key Context
    The keys are programmed into the AES core by an APB interface. The following steps describe how to
    program a key context to the firmware:
        1.    Write the Key Value into the KEY_x registers.


                  Note      Key must be written in big endian format.



        2.    Select the key context which will be programmed by writing the KEY_IDX.
        3.    Poll KEY_LOAD_STAT.BUSY register. This is only asserted during key installation that is
              roundabout 30 core clock cycles, until it is 0. Alternatively, use key done interrupt to check if key
              installation is finished.
        4.    To program more keys go to step 2.
        5.    Go to step 3, if all keys are already programmed.

2.9.1.1            Key Context Mapping
    The mapping of the AES-GCM contexts versus the RX and TX security association index, is performed as
    follows:
         n    KEY_IDX = 0, ENCRYPT = 1: programs the key used for the TX SC#0, SA#0 (SA#0, corresponds to
              AN = 0)



Version 6585-001                                               Synopsys, Inc.                          SolvNetPlus     77
March 2025                                                                                             Synopsys IP
Architecture                                                       MACsec Single Port Automotive Compliant (AC) Security Module Databook



         n     KEY_IDX = 1, ENCRYPT = 1: programs the key used for the TX SC#0, SA#1 (SA#1, corresponds to
               AN = 1)
         n     KEY_IDX = 2, ENCRYPT = 1: programs the key used for the TX SC#1, SA#0
         n     KEY_IDX = 3, ENCRYPT = 1: programs the key used for the TX SC#1, SA#1
         n     …
         n     KEY_IDX = N, ENCRYPT = 1: programs the key used for the TX SC#N, SA#1
         n     KEY_IDX = N+1, ENCRYPT = 0: programs the key used for the RX SA#0
         n     KEY_IDX = N+2, ENCRYPT = 0: programs the key used for the RX SA#1
         n     KEY_IDX = N+3, ENCRYPT = 0: programs the key used for the RX SA#2
         n     KEY_IDX = N+3, ENCRYPT = 0: programs the key used for the RX SA#3
         n     ...
     The application must program the CTRL register of the AES-GCM core as per the described mapping. The
     application must program not only the KEY_IDX, but also the ENCRYPT bit, which indicates if the context is
     used for encryption or decryption and the KEY_SZ field that will indicate the size of the key.


                   Note     The complete CTRL register must be programmed as indicated above for every context/SA.



2.9.2           Changing a Key for an SA
     The DWC_macsec allows key swapping through multiple ways. You can select any one of the following
     options.
         n     Swapping between ANs for a given SA:
               q     The application has one AN that is active and the other that is inactive.
               q     Program a new key the inactive SA AN. For detailed steps, see “Programming a Key Context” on
                     page 77.
               q     Set this newly programmed SA AN as active.
               q     Set the initially active SA AN as inactive.
         n     Not swapping between ANs for a given SA:
               q     The application has all ANs active for a given SA.
               q     Application halts the traffic associated to the specific SA AN.
               q     Set the specific SA AN to inactive.
               q     Program a new key for that specific SA AN. For detailed steps, see “Programming a Key Context”
                     on page 77.
               q     Set the specific SA AN to active.

2.10          Host Configuration Interface - APB Interface
    The APB4 interface follows the AMBA defined standard. The integrator addresses the ARM IHI 0024C -
    AMBA 4 APB Protocol.
    The APB interface for the DWC_macsec, uses the PPROT[1] bit to protect access to the complete address
    space.

2.11          Parity and ECC Support
2.11.1        Parity Support
    The AES-GCM present in the DWC_macsec, offers parity protection on the configuration registers. For the
    integrator to make usage of this parity feature, it need to enable the specific interrupt by the AES-GCM APB
    interface. The parity failure interrupt is forwarded to the O_aes_hcfg_irq.

2.13.2        Controlled and Uncontrolled Ports Frame Processing
    In the 802.1AE standard, the processing behavior of MACsec AC and non-MACsec frames are described
    depending if a controlled or uncontrolled port is addressed.
    Since the DWC_macsec is unaware if the physical port is connected only to a controlled port or to both
    controlled and uncontrolled ports, several configuration options increase the flexibility for the integrator to
    deal with both scenarios.
    In addition to the regular security association rule checking imposed by the TX/RX SAI and TX/RX SAD
    lookups, the DWC_macsec contains the following options when non-MACsec frames are mentioned ( this is
    any type of frame that does not have the 0x88e5 ethertype):
        n    Global Validate Configuration - configured through the MIB_VALIDATE register
             q     This allows the user to apply a rule check for the following:
                   n   non-MACsec frames
                   n   MACsec AC frames that do not match a lookup search and have the C bit = 0
             q     If it is set to non-strict, any of the above-mentioned frames are bypassed (without being
                   modified).
             q     If it is set to strict, the following happens:
                   n   the non-MACsec frames with ethertypes that match the ETHERTYPE_FILTER_x are bypassed
                   n   the non-MACsec frames with ethertypes that do not match the ETHERTYPE_FILTER_x are
                       discarded
                   n   the MACsec AC frames that do not match a lookup search and have the C bit = 0 are
                       discarded
        n    Non-MACsec frame valid Ethertype - configured through the ETHERTYPE_FILTER_x and
             ethertype_filter_en register fields
             q     This is a lookup that contains up to 8 programmable ethertypes.
             q     If the Global Validate Configuration is set to strict, then the non-MACsec frames are parsed
                   against this lookup. If there is a match, the frame is bypassed; if there is no match the frame is
                   dropped.
        n    Global MACsec AC Tagging Enable - configured through the replace_ethertype register field
             q     When enabled, it replaces the 0x88e5 ethertype with a proprietary ethertype one of the MACsec
                   AC frames that are processed in the RX, and passes all checks.
             q     The frame is received by the application on the RX with the SecTAG. Within the SecTAG, the
                   application checks this proprietary ethertype (ICV is nonetheless removed).
    Table 2-11 represents the behavior corresponding to the global configuration along with the MACsec AC
    frames protocol parsing (the values configured on the RX security association lookup):

2.13.3       Behavior Under Error Conditions
    The DWC_macsec implements the behavior described in this section that is applicable for the error conditions specified in Table 2-10 (that may occur
    due to protocol errors or wrong programming):

2.13.3.1        On TX/Egress
        n    Frame is poisoned with CRC error if HARD_TTL limit is reached.
        n    A RUNT frame is discarded or dropped if it has less than 64 bytes (excluding preamble and terminate control character).
        n    Frame is truncated, and CRC is poisoned if the MTU limit is hit.
        n    Frame is encrypted and CRC sent to the PCS is poisoned, if a frame is received from the MAC with a CRC error.
        n    Frame is discarded or dropped, if a frame matches an Security Association that is inactive.



 Version 6585-001                                                                Synopsys, Inc.                                                           SolvNetPlus       85
 March 2025                                                                                                                                               Synopsys IP
Architecture                                                    MACsec Single Port Automotive Compliant (AC) Security Module Databook



         n     Frame is encrypted but CRC poisoned if the size is larger than what has been programmed for the
               specific Security Association.

2.13.3.2           On RX/Ingress
         n     Frame CRC is poisoned, if an ICV error is detected.
         n     Frame CRC is poisoned, if the Security Association is inactive.
         n     Frame CRC is poisoned, if a SecTAG error is detected.
         n     Frame CRC is poisoned, if a Replay Error is detected.
         n     Frame CRC is poisoned, if an AES-GCM Security Association does not have a key installed (due to
               ICV check failure).
         n     Frame is discarded/dropped if an IPG violation is detected.
         n     A RUNT frame is discarded/dropped if it has less than 64 bytes (excluding preamble and terminate
               control character).
         n     Frame is passed through to the MAC if the Security Association is not present in the RX SAI LUT.
         n     Frame is decrypted and CRC sent to the MAC is poisoned, if a frame is received from the PCS with a
               CRC error.

                          Ethernet standard guarantees an Ethernet minimum frame total size of 64 bytes, hence if a
                   Note   frame is smaller and needs nonetheless to be transmitted, the MAC or application must add
                          padding. The DWC_macsec IP does not add padding to the frames or process frames with an
                          SL byte different from 0.



2.14           FIPS 140-3 Test Mode Usage
     The DWC_macsec contains an AES-centric test mode, that enables the integrator to evaluate or test the
     algorithm implementation of the cryptographic core. This test mode is used by the integrator to perform the
     algorithm testing which is required to achieve a FIPS certification. The test mode is available when the
     DWC_MACSEC_AES_FIPS_EN parameter is set to 1.
     The DWC_macsec has the following test modes:
         n     BIST mode
         n     Firmware driven (FW) test mode

2.14.1         BIST Mode
     The BIST mode runs automatically after the core reset is released. To use the BIST mode, the integrator must
     perform the following:
       1.      Reset the DWC_macsec.
       2.      Poll the done flag through the following options:
               q    Monitor the O_aes_fips_self_test_done output signal until it is asserted to 1’b1.
               q    Poll the FIPS_SELF_TEST_STAT.SELF_TEST_DONE_APB field until it is asserted to 1’b1.




86      SolvNetPlus                                     Synopsys, Inc.                                              Version 6585-001
        Synopsys IP                                                                                                       March 2025
MACsec Single Port Automotive Compliant (AC) Security Module Databook                                                     Architecture



       3.    Check the fail status through the following options:
             q     Monitor the O_aes_fips_self_test_fail output signal.
             q     Read the FIPS_SELF_TEST_STAT.FAIL register field.
       4.    If a failure occurred, read the FIPS_SELF_TEST_STAT.FAIL_CAUSE register to identify the reason
             for the failure.
       5.    In case of failure, it is possible to inhibit the output of the AES-GCM (making the AES-GCM
             unusable) through the following options:
             q     Assert the I_aes_fips_inhib input pin to 1’b1.
             q     Set the MISC_CONFIG.INHIB_OUTPUT register field to 1’b1.
    It is possible to re-run the BIST after the core is in mission mode.

                           The DWC_macsec does not perform data back pressuring automatically, therefore it
                 Note      is up to the integrator’s responsibility to guarantee that there is no data corruption in
                           the process (BIST must run when there is no application data).


    To re-trigger the BIST, the integrator must perform the following steps:
       1.    Inhibit AES-GCM output through one of the two options:
             q     assert the I_aes_fips_inhibit input signal to 1’1b
             q     write 1’b1 to the MISC_CONFIG.INHIBIT_OUTPUT register field
       2.    Enable test mode by writing 1’b1 to the FIPS_SELF_TEST_CTL.FIPS_SELF_TEST_ENA register
             field.
       3.    Setup BIST_VECT_MODE register:
             q     The FUNCT field selects the test operation.
                   n    0: Batch (runs all tests)
                   n    1: CTR tests
                   n    2: GCM tests
                   n    3: ECB

                 Note      If the Batch operation is selected, the remaining fields of this register are irrelevant.



             q     The KEY_SIZE field sets the key size to use.
                   n    0: 128-bit key
                   n    1: 256-bit. This field is only used if 256-bit keys are enabled
                        (DWC_MACSEC_MAX_KEY_SIZE==1)
             q     The ENCRYPT sets the operation direction. Set it to 0 to decrypt and set it to 1 to encrypt.
       4.    To test the error injection, set the BIST_VECT_ERR_INJ register.




Version 6585-001                                               Synopsys, Inc.                                      SolvNetPlus     87
March 2025                                                                                                         Synopsys IP
Architecture                                                     MACsec Single Port Automotive Compliant (AC) Security Module Databook



               q   By setting the ECB_ERR_INJ, MAC_ERR_INJ, GCM_ERR_INJ, and CTR_ERR_INJ fields, a bit-flip
                   is inserted in the respective test vectors to execute the error testing.
       5.      Clear the FIPS_SELF_TEST_STAT.SELF_TEST_DONE flag and write 1’b1 to the
               FIPS_SELF_TEST_STAT.SELF_TEST_FAIL register field.
       6.      Trigger the test by writing 1’b1 to the BIST_VECT_CTL.BIST_TEST_GO field (this field is self-
               clearing).
       7.      Poll the done status through the following options:
               q   Monitor the O_aes_fips_self_test_done output signal until it is asserted to 1’b1.
               q   Poll the FIPS_SELF_TEST_STAT.SELF_TEST_DONE APB register field until is asserted to 1’b1.
       8.      Check the fail status through the following options:
               q   Monitor the O_aes_fips_self_test_fail output.
               q   Read the FIPS_SELF_TEST_STAT.FAIL register field.
       9.      In case of failure, read the FIPS_SELF_TEST_STAT.FAIL_CAUSE register to identify the reason for
               the failure.
               q   If the GCM decrypt test or batch test is run, read also the
                   FIPS_SELF_TEST_STAT.SELF_TEST_MATCH_RES register. A 1’b1 indicates a proper match for
                   the MAC. If it is 1’b0, this means there is a failure in the MAC comparison.
      10.      Disable test mode by setting the FIPS_SELF_TEST_CTL.FIPS_SELF_TEST_ENA register field to
               1’b0.
      11.      If the test is passed, deassert the output inhibition in the same way it is asserted:
               q   By deasserting the I_aes_fips_inhibit input signal to 1’b0.
               q   By writing MISC_CONFIG.INHIBIT_OUTPUT register field to 1’b0.

2.14.2         Firmware (FW) Driven Test Mode
     The FW-driven test mode allows the integrator to run its specific test vectors. In this test mode, the AES-
     GCM inputs are driven by a set of APB-accessible registers, where the integrator can drive the required test
     vectors.
     Perform the following steps to use the FW-driven test mode:
       1.      Inhibit the AES output through one of the following options:
               q   Assert the I_aes_fips_inhibit input signal to 1’b1.
               q   Write 1’b1 to the MISC_CONFIG.INHIBIT_OUTPUT register field.
       2.      Enable test mode by writing 1’b1 to the FIPS_SELF_TEST_CTL.FIPS_SELF_TEST_ENA register
               field.
       3.      (Optional) Enable the internal self-checker by setting the
               FIPS_SELF_TEST_CTL.FIPS_SELF_TEST_CHECK register field.




88      SolvNetPlus                                      Synopsys, Inc.                                              Version 6585-001
        Synopsys IP                                                                                                        March 2025
MACsec Single Port Automotive Compliant (AC) Security Module Databook                                        Architecture



       4.    Load the AES key in the same way as in mission mode:

                          n   Load the test mode key into a specific context. Both the
                 Note         FIPS_SELF_TEST_VECT_CMD_CTX register and the
                              DWC_MACSEC_AES_DEFAULT_FIPS_CTX_IDX parameter indicate which context
                              to load the key into.
                          n   For CTR mode tests the key must be loaded with the CTRL.MODE register field set
                              to 1.


       5.    Load the IV into the FIPS_SELF_TEST_IVx registers (GCM and CTR modes only):
             q     The most significant word goes into the IV0 register.
             q     In GCM mode, the IV is 96-bit wide, so write the IV3 register to 0.
       6.    Load the Additional Authentication Data (AAD) and message (MSG) vectors:
             q     Write the AAD (fulfilling the size indicated by the DWC_MACSEC_AES_DP_WIDTH bits) into
                   FIPS_SELF_TEST_IDATAx registers (most significant word goes into the IDATA0 register, AAD
                   is only present in GCM mode).
             q     Write MSG (fulfilling the size indicated by the DWC_MACSEC_AES_MSG_WIDTH bits) into the
                   remaining FIPS_SELF_TEST_IDATAx registers (MSG and AAD must not share the same 128-bit
                   block, the most significant word goes into register IDATA0, 4, 8, and so on).
                          n   AAD+MSG must not exceed DWC_MACSEC_AES_DP_WIDTH bits.
                 Note
                          n   The number of AAD or MSG bits should be byte-aligned.



       7.    Load the FIPS_SELF_TEST_ATT register.
             q     Set the SELF_TEST_AAD field to 1’b1 if the data path contains AAD.
             q     Set the SELF_TEST_MSG field to 1’b1 if the data path contains MSG.
             q     (Optional) Set the SELF_TEST_MAC_MATCH field to 1’b1 to use the MAC checker (if the checker is
                   enabled in step 3). This checker is used during the last round (SELF_TEST_EOP ==1) of GCM
                   decryption operations.
             q     Set the SELF_TEST_ECB field to 1’b1 when in ECB mode.
             q     Set the SELF_TEST_SOP field to 1’b1 during the first round of the packet (first portion of the
                   vector).
             q     Set the SELF_TEST_EOP field to 1’b1 during the last round (the entire vector has been written).
       8.    (Optional) Load AAD and expected cipher or plain text vectors only if the internal self-checker is
             activated in step 3.
             q     Load expected AAD and cipher or plain text vectors into FIPS_SELF_TEST_ODATAx registers
                   the same way as in step 6.
       9.    (Optional) Load expected MAC vector only if the internal MAC checker is enabled in step 3.
     10.     Load AAD and MSG sizes:




Version 6585-001                                               Synopsys, Inc.                         SolvNetPlus     89
March 2025                                                                                            Synopsys IP
Architecture                                                      MACsec Single Port Automotive Compliant (AC) Security Module Databook



               q   If the current round contains AAD (FIPS_SELF_TEST_ATT.SELF_TEST_AAD == 1), load the
                   AAD size (in bytes) into the FIPS_SELF_TEST_AAD_SIZE register. A zero in this register means
                   DWC_MACSEC_AES_DP_WIDTH of 8 bytes.
               q   If the current round contains MSG (FIPS_SELF_TEST_ATT.SELF_TEST_MSG == 1), load the
                   MSG size (in bytes) into the FIPS_SELF_TEST_MSG_SIZE register.
      11.      Load total AAD and MSG length (GCM mode only):
               q   This is only required during the last round of a multi-round packet (eop==1 && sop==0).
               q   Write the following into the FIPS_SELF_TEST_IVx: {tot_aad_len[47:0], 12’h0,
                   tot_msg_len[35:0]} registers.
               q   Most significant word goes into the IV0 register. IV3 register is set to all zeros.
      12.      Clear the done and fail status fields by writing 1’b1 into the following fields:
               q   FIPS_SELF_TEST_STAT.SELF_TEST_DONE
               q   FIPS_SELF_TEST_STAT.SELF_TEST_FAIL
      13.      Trigger the test by writing 1’b1 to FIPS_SELF_TEST_VECT_CTL.SELF_TEST_GO field (this field is
               self-clearing).
      14.      Poll the done status through the following options:
               q   Monitor the O_aes_fips_self_test_done output signal until is set to 1’b1.
               q   Poll the FIPS_SELF_TEST_STAT.SELF_TEST_DONE register field until is set to 1’b1.
      15.      Read fail status through the following options:
               q   O_aes_fips_self_test_fail output signal
               q   FIPS_SELF_TEST_STAT.SELF_TEST_FAIL register field
               q   In case the MAC checker is enabled, the
                   FIPS_SELF_TEST_STAT.SELF_TEST_MAC_MATCH_RES register field indicates its result: 1’b0
                   means that it did not match, 1’b1 means that it did match
      16.      Read the FIPS_SELF_TEST_ODATAx registers and check if the cipher or plain is the expected one.
      17.      Read the FIPS_SELF_TEST_MACx registers and check if the MAC is the expected (GCM only). This
               is only done during the last round of the packet (eop==1).
      18.      If an error occurs, the test ends, and the output is left inhibited (disabling the AES usage).
      19.      Clear the FIPS_SELF_TEST_STAT register by writing 1’b1 to the fields (fields are W1C).
      20.      Repeat from step 6 until the entire vectors are injected.
      21.      Repeat from step 5 until all vectors are tested.
      22.      Disable test mode by setting the FIPS_SELF_TEST_CTL.FIPS_SELF_TEST_ENA register field to
               1’b0.
      23.      If the test is passed, deassert the output inhibition in the same way it is asserted:
               q   By setting the I_aes_fips_inhibit input signal to ‘1b0.




90      SolvNetPlus                                      Synopsys, Inc.                                               Version 6585-001
        Synopsys IP                                                                                                         March 2025
MACsec Single Port Automotive Compliant (AC) Security Module Databook                                     Architecture



             q     By writing the MISC_CONFIG.INHIBIT_OUTPUT register field to 1’b0.
                          An On-demand BIST test must be executed before any FW-driven test. If the
                 Note     integrator needs to execute a new BIST test after a FW-driven one, the DWC_macsec
                          must be reset.


2.15          SRAM Zeroization
    When external SRAMs are used, the DWC_macsec contains an SRAM zeroization functionality that allows
    for all external SRAMs to be written with 0s. This feature is meant to be used during the initialization of the
    DWC_macsec (for example, to be done after BIST finishes). The zeroization feature is available when
    DWC_MACSEC_SRAM_ZERO_EN is set.
    To perform the SRAM zeroization, the following steps should be performed:
       1.    Reset the DWC_macsec.
       2.    Wait for the reset phase to complete.
       3.    Assert the I_sram_zero_init input signal to 1’b1.
       4.    Wait until the output signal O_sram_zero_done gets deasserted to 1’b0 and then deassert the input
             signal I_sram_zero_init to 1’b0.
       5.    Wait for the signal O_sram_zero_done to be asserted to 1’b1 (signaling that the zeroization process
             is terminated).

3.2            Performance Considerations
    The DWC_macsec supports full throughput that matches the link speed. The throughput matching is achieved by selecting the
    DWC_MACSEC_PERF_RATE parameter value.

MACsec Single Port Automotive Compliant (AC) Security Module Databook                                  Signal Descriptions




                                                                                                                   5
                                                                                Signal Descriptions
    This chapter details all possible I/O signals in the controller. For configurable IP titles, your actual
    configuration might not contain all of these signals.
    Inputs are on the left of the signal diagrams; outputs are on the right.
    Attention: For configurable IP titles, do not use this document to determine the exact I/O footprint of the
    controller. It is for reference purposes only.
    When you configure the controller in coreConsultant, you must access the I/O signals for your actual
    configuration at workspace/report/IO.html or workspace/report/IO.xml after you have completed the
    report creation activity. That report comes from the exact same source as this chapter but removes all the
    I/O signals that are not in your actual configuration. This does not apply to non-configurable IP titles. In
    addition, all parameter expressions are evaluated to actual values. Therefore, the widths might change
    depending on your actual configuration.
    Some expressions might refer to TCL functions or procedures (sometimes identified as <functionof>) that
    coreConsultant uses to make calculations. The exact formula used by these TCL functions is not provided in
    this chapter. However, when you configure the controller in coreConsultant, all TCL functions and
    parameters are evaluated completely; and the resulting values are displayed where appropriate in the
    coreConsultant GUI reports.
    In addition to describing the function of each signal, the signal descriptions in this chapter include the
    following information:
    Active State: Indicates whether the signal is active high or active low. When a signal is not intended to be
    used in a particular application, then this signal needs to be tied or driven to the inactive state (opposite of
    the active state).
    Registered: Indicates whether or not the signal is registered directly inside the IP boundary without
    intervening logic (excluding simple buffers). A value of No does not imply that the signal is not
    synchronous, only that there is some combinatorial logic between the signal's origin or destination register
    and the boundary of the controller. A value of N/A indicates that this information is not provided for this IP
    title.
    Synchronous to: Indicates which clocks in the IP sample this input (drive for an output) when considering
    all possible configurations. A particular configuration might not have all of the clocks listed. This clock
    might not be the same as the clock that your application logic should use to clock (sample/drive) this pin.
    For more details, consult the clock section in the databook. The presence of the postfix SuperList indicates a
    list of all possible clocks over all possible configs. Consult coreConsultant report for which clock applies to
    your specific configuration.
